# Open set condition

 [Add links](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Special:EntityPage/Q110933486#sitelinks-wikipedia)                          From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia   Condition for fractals in math [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Open_set_condition.png/250px-Open_set_condition.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Open_set_condition.png)an open set covering of the [sierpinski triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierpinski_triangle) along with one of its mappings ψ*i*.

In [fractal geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractal_geometry), the **open set condition** (**OSC**) is a commonly imposed condition on self-similar fractals. In some sense, the condition imposes restrictions on the overlap in a fractal construction.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_set_condition#cite_note-1) Specifically, given an [iterated function system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iterated_function_system) of [contractive mappings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contraction_mapping)      ψ  1   , … ,  ψ  m     {\displaystyle \psi _{1},\ldots ,\psi _{m}}  , the open set condition requires that there exists a nonempty, open set V satisfying two conditions:

1. ⋃  i = 1   m    ψ  i   ( V ) ⊆ V ,   {\displaystyle \bigcup _{i=1}^{m}\psi _{i}(V)\subseteq V,}
2. The sets      ψ  1   ( V ) , … ,  ψ  m   ( V )   {\displaystyle \psi _{1}(V),\ldots ,\psi _{m}(V)}   are pairwise disjoint.

Introduced in 1946 by P.A.P Moran,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_set_condition#cite_note-2) the open set condition is used to compute the dimensions of certain self-similar fractals, notably the Sierpinski Gasket. It is also used to simplify computation of the packing measure.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_set_condition#cite_note-3)

An equivalent statement of the open set condition is to require that the s-dimensional [Hausdorff measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_measure) of the set is greater than zero.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_set_condition#cite_note-4)

## Computing Hausdorff dimension

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_set_condition&action=edit&section=1)]

When the open set condition holds and each      ψ  i     {\displaystyle \psi _{i}}   is a similitude (that is, a composition of an [isometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isometry) and a [dilation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dilation_(metric_space)) around some point), then the unique fixed point of     ψ   {\displaystyle \psi }   is a set whose [Hausdorff dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_dimension) is the unique solution for *s* of the following:[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_set_condition#cite_note-5)

      ∑  i = 1   m    r  i   s   = 1.   {\displaystyle \sum _{i=1}^{m}r_{i}^{s}=1.}

where ri is the magnitude of the dilation of the similitude.

With this theorem, the Hausdorff dimension of the Sierpinski gasket can be calculated. Consider three [non-collinear points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-collinear_points) *a*1, *a*2, *a*3 in the plane **R**2 and let      ψ  i     {\displaystyle \psi _{i}}   be the dilation of ratio 1/2 around *ai*. The unique non-empty fixed point of the corresponding mapping     ψ   {\displaystyle \psi }   is a Sierpinski gasket, and the dimension *s* is the unique solution of

       (   1 2   )   s   +   (   1 2   )   s   +   (   1 2   )   s   = 3   (   1 2   )   s   = 1.   {\displaystyle \left({\frac {1}{2}}\right)^{s}+\left({\frac {1}{2}}\right)^{s}+\left({\frac {1}{2}}\right)^{s}=3\left({\frac {1}{2}}\right)^{s}=1.}

Taking [natural logarithms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_logarithm) of both sides of the above equation, we can solve for *s*, that is: *s* = ln(3)/ln(2). The Sierpinski gasket is self-similar and satisfies the OSC.

## Strong open set condition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_set_condition&action=edit&section=2)]

The strong open set condition (SOSC) is an extension of the open set condition. A fractal F satisfies the SOSC if, in addition to satisfying the OSC, the intersection between F and the open set V is nonempty.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_set_condition#cite_note-6) The two conditions are equivalent for self-similar and self-conformal sets, but not for certain classes of other sets, such as function systems with infinite mappings and in non-euclidean metric spaces.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_set_condition#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_set_condition#cite_note-8) In these cases, SOCS is indeed a stronger condition.
